draft.title: Polynomial and power graphs
card: Polynomial
a function such as y = x³ − 4x, with whole-number powers of x. Its domain is all real numbers and its graph has no asymptotes.
Intercepts
The y-intercept is found by putting x = 0. The x-intercepts are found by solving y = 0. For y = x³ − 4x, x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0, so x = −2, 0 or 2.
Power function
y = x^n with n negative, such as y = 1/x², has the asymptotes x = 0 and y = 0. Its domain leaves out x = 0. A square root such as y = √x is also a power function, with domain x ≥ 0.
Stationary points
These are points where the gradient is 0. A stationary point of inflection also has a curve that changes concavity, as in y = x³ at (0, 0). A cubic can have two turning points or none.
draft.remember: Polynomials have no asymptotes and a domain of all reals. Negative powers have asymptotes and leave out x = 0.

a.q: What are the x-intercepts of y = x³ − 9x?
a.why: Factorise: x(x − 3)(x + 3) = 0, so x = −3, 0 or 3. The option 0 and 9 comes from stopping at x² = 9 and mistaking it for x = 9.
a.clue: Take out a common factor of x first, then factorise what is left.

b.q: Which function has a vertical asymptote at x = 0?
b.why: A negative power puts x in the denominator, so x = 0 is not allowed and the graph rises or falls without limit near it. Polynomials have no asymptotes. The graph of y = √x starts at (0, 0), so it has no asymptote.
b.clue: Look for the function where x = 0 is not in the domain.

final.title: Polynomial and power graphs
card: Polynomial
a function such as \(y = x^{3} - 4x\), with whole-number powers of \(x\). Its domain is all real numbers and its graph has no asymptotes.
Intercepts
The y-intercept is found by putting \(x = 0\). The x-intercepts are found by solving \(y = 0\). For \(y = x^{3} - 4x\), \(x(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0\), so \(x = -2\), \(x = 0\) or \(x = 2\).
Power function

\(y = x^{n}\) with \(n\) negative, such as \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\), has the asymptotes \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Its domain leaves out \(x = 0\). A square root such as \(y = \sqrt{x}\) is also a power function, with domain \(x \ge 0\).
Stationary points
These are points where the gradient is 0. A stationary point of inflection also has a curve that changes concavity, as in \(y = x^{3}\) at \((0, 0)\). A cubic can have two turning points or none.

2.alt: The cubic \(y = x^{3} - 4x\). It crosses the x-axis at \(x = -2\), \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\), and the origin is also its y-intercept.

3.alt: The graph of \(y = \frac{1}{x^{2}}\). It has no point at \(x = 0\). Both branches are above the x-axis, rising without limit near \(x = 0\) and getting closer to \(y = 0\) as \(x\) grows, so its asymptotes are \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\).

final.remember: Polynomials have no asymptotes and a domain of all reals. Negative powers have asymptotes and leave out \(x = 0\).

a.q: What are the x-intercepts of \(y = x^{3} - 9x\)?
a.why: Factorise: \(x(x - 3)(x + 3) = 0\), so \(x = -3\), \(x = 0\) or \(x = 3\). The option 0 and 9 comes from stopping at \(x^{2} = 9\) and mistaking it for \(x = 9\).
a.clue: Take out a common factor of \(x\) first, then factorise what is left.

b.q: Which function has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\)?
b.why: A negative power puts \(x\) in the denominator, so \(x = 0\) is not allowed and the graph rises or falls without limit near it. Polynomials have no asymptotes. The graph of \(y = \sqrt{x}\) starts at \((0, 0)\), so it has no asymptote.
b.clue: Look for the function where \(x = 0\) is not in the domain.
